newsitem.title: FRANCE: Summary of French bill to allow private pensions.
newsitem.headline: Summary of French bill to allow private pensions.

text.p: The following is a summary of the main provisions of draft legislation to allow private pension funds in France.
Private pension funds will be voluntary, offered at company or at sectoral level and employers have the option to supplement contributions of employees but funds are to be managed externally.
Investment by pension funds in fixed-income bonds will be capped at 65 percent, a measure taken to encourage investment in France's weakly capitalised stock market.
Contributors can withdraw a maximum of 20 percent in lump-sum at retirement age, the rest to be drawn on as annuities.
Pension funds to be managed by banks, insurers, provident societies, mutual or other such groups.

Those who manage pension funds must cordon them off from the parent company for prudential reasons and will be subject to control by the Bourse authorities. The government wanted this to be optional but the Senate wants it made mandatory.

Investment by funds in any one company's stock to be capped. The Senate adopted an amendment on January 30 setting the cap at five percent of a company's capital, while the National Assembly text sets the cap at 10 percent.

Funds are obliged to vote at shareholder meetings of companies where they are stakeholders, to avoid a conflict of interest between fund and group it belongs to, for example in case the group it belongs to also has stake in the given company. This was added in the Senate second reading and yet to be confirmed.
Defined benefit payout schemes would be prohibited under a Senate amendment designed to help promote equity investment.

Employees will be free to contribute or not to a fund, to suspend and restart without penalty and transfer rights on termination of a job contract or transfer rights to a surviving partner, child or infirm person in the event of death.

Employees can sign up to a fund outside their employing company where there no collective agreement at company. Senate second reading text says this should apply if a company fails within a year to reach a collective pension agreement, while National Assembly second reading text envisaged two-year waiting period.
Employee contributions qualify for write off against income tax to the tune of five percent of annual gross salary or 20 percent of the prevailing social security system ceiling.
Employers can contribute up to a maximum of four times the level of employee's contributions.
Employer contributions deductible for purposes of company tax and exempt from social security charges.

While the text does not allow for pension funds to recover corporate dividend tax, Finance Minister Jean Arthuis told the Senate he would "consider" the issue amid concern that funds might otherwise be tempted to invest in equities in other countries where they would be entitled to this.

NOTE -- The bill was approved in a second Senate reading on January 30 after second a reading in the National Assembly, the lower house of parliament, and set for arbitration in a mixed Senate-Assembly on February 5.
